content: Neonatal herpes is a herpes virus infection that an infant acquires during birth. Symptoms of Neonatal Herpes: Herpes may present as a localized skin infection. Small, fluid-filled blisters (vesicles) can appear, which rupture, crust over, and heal, sometimes leaving mild scarring. The infection can disseminate throughout the body (disseminated herpes), potentially affecting multiple organs. When the brain is involved, it is termed herpes encephalitis. The liver, lungs, and kidneys may also be affected. Skin blisters may or may not be present in disseminated herpes. Newborns with herpes that has spread to the brain or other organs are often critically ill. Symptoms include: Easy bleeding Breathing difficulties, such as rapid breathing (tachypnea), grunting, nostril flaring, or episodes of apnea (temporary cessation of breathing) Cyanosis (bluish skin) Lethargy Hypothermia (low body temperature) Poor feeding Jaundice Seizures Shock Coma Skin lesions, including fluid-filled blisters Herpes acquired shortly after birth presents with symptoms similar to those of birth-acquired herpes. Intrauterine herpes (infection during pregnancy) can result in: Eye disease, such as chorioretinitis (inflammation of the retina) Severe brain damage Skin lesions Causes of Neonatal Herpes: Newborns can contract herpes virus through: Intrauterine transmission (very rare) Passage through the birth canal (the most common mode of infection) Postpartum exposure, such as contact with someone who has active herpes mouth sores (e.g., through kissing) Risk Factors: Infants are at higher risk if the mother has an active genital herpes infection during delivery. Some mothers may be unaware of internal herpes sores (inside the vagina) or a past herpes infection. Herpes simplex virus type 2 (genital herpes) is the most common cause of neonatal herpes, but herpes simplex virus type 1 (oral herpes) can also be transmitted. Diagnostic Tests: Tests for birth-acquired herpes include: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test from vesicle scrapings Electroencephalogram (EEG) MRI of the head Spinal fluid culture Vesicle culture Additional tests for critically ill infants may include: Blood gas analysis Coagulation studies (PT, PTT) Complete blood count Electrolyte measurements Liver function tests When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If your baby shows any symptoms of birth-acquired herpes, including skin lesions alone, seek immediate medical attention. Treatment Options: Neonatal herpes is typically treated with intravenous antiviral medications, most commonly acyclovir. Treatment may need to continue for several weeks. Supportive therapies may be required to manage complications such as seizures or shock. Critically ill infants are often treated in an intensive care unit. Prognosis: Infants with systemic herpes or encephalitis often have poor outcomes despite early antiviral treatment. Infants with skin-limited disease may experience recurrent vesicles even after treatment, which can increase the risk of learning disabilities and may require further management. Possible Complications: Secondary bacterial or fungal infections of skin lesions Coma Death Developmental delays Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) causing excessive bleeding Eye problems, such as chorioretinitis or keratitis Gastrointestinal issues, including diarrhea Hepatitis Jaundice Liver failure Lung problems, such as pneumonia or pneumonitis Neurological complications, including seizures and developmental delays Respiratory distress Shock Skin lesions Prevention of Neonatal Herpes: Pregnant women should inform their healthcare provider if they have a history of genital herpes. Practicing safer sex can reduce the risk of acquiring genital herpes during pregnancy. Mothers who are not infected with herpes cannot transmit the virus to their baby during delivery. Individuals with active cold sores (herpes labialis) should avoid contact with newborns. Caregivers with cold sores should wear surgical masks and practice strict hand hygiene before handling the infant to prevent transmission. Mothers should consult their healthcare provider to discuss strategies to minimize the risk of transmitting herpes to their baby.
